# Use cases

Five workflows, end to end. Each one is a real sequence of commands with the
output you should expect — start with the first even if another is closer to
what you want, because the rest assume it.

## 1. The morning triage

**You want:** ten minutes with today's papers, without spending quota on ones
you would have skipped anyway.

The trick is two passes. Look first, summarize second.

```bash
uv run papertracker --no-summarize --days 2
```

This runs the full pipeline — fetch, dedup, local relevance scoring — and prints
matches sorted by score, spending nothing. Scores are colored by band, so you
can judge the cutoff at a glance:

```text
  0.812  Learned Force Fields for Molecular Dynamics at Scale  ★ NeurIPS
        arxiv · NeurIPS · 2026-08-08 · https://arxiv.org/abs/...

  0.694  Message Passing Networks with Equivariant Attention
        arxiv · n/a · 2026-08-08 · https://arxiv.org/abs/...

  0.601  A Survey of Graph Pooling Operators
        crossref · TPAMI · 2026-08-07 · https://doi.org/...
```

<!-- SCREENSHOT SLOT: terminal-triage.png — see docs/images/README.md
<img src="images/terminal-triage.png"
     alt="Terminal listing of scored papers, each with a color-coded relevance score, title, priority-venue badge, source, and link."
     width="820">
-->

If the top of that list looks right, summarize — and pick papers individually
rather than taking all of them:

```bash
uv run papertracker --select --days 2
```

That opens a browser tab on `127.0.0.1`. Tick the papers worth summarizing and
set a template per paper. The dropdown lists the `abstract` templates — this is
a triage pass over abstracts, so the full-text formats belong to
[step 2](#2-deep-reading-a-shortlist) and are not offered here.

<!-- SCREENSHOT SLOT: selector-daily.png — see docs/images/README.md
<img src="images/selector-daily.png"
     alt="The --select browser page: one row per paper with a checkbox, a colored relevance score badge, the title and venue, and a per-paper template dropdown."
     width="820">
-->

Output lands in `user_data/digests/<project-id>/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, grouped by
priority venues first.

**If the list is empty or noisy**, that is a tuning problem, not a bug — see
[Relevance filter](configuration.md#relevance-filter). Sharpening
`topic_statement` beats changing the threshold.

## 2. Deep-reading a shortlist

**You want:** proper summaries of papers you have already collected and decided
to read, from their full PDFs rather than their abstracts.

Daily digests are abstract-based. For full text, PaperTracker reads PDFs out of
your Zotero library. Point it at a collection by the path shown in Zotero's
sidebar:

```text
My Library
├── Reading
│   ├── Deep Reading          →  "Reading/Deep Reading"
│   └── Skimmed
└── Inbox
```

<!-- SCREENSHOT SLOT: zotero-collections.png — see docs/images/README.md
<img src="images/zotero-collections.png"
     alt="Zotero's sidebar showing a nested collection tree, with the Reading/Deep Reading collection selected."
     width="420">
-->

```bash
uv run papertracker --list-zotero-collections
uv run papertracker --zotero-collection "Reading/Deep Reading" --template deep-technical
```

Text is extracted locally, page labels preserved, and processed in bounded
chunks before the template is filled. Your library is opened read-only and never
modified — details in [Zotero PDF batch mode](zotero.md).

Use a `fulltext` template here. `deep-technical` suits methods papers,
`deep-human-study` suits user studies, `deep-synthesis` suits surveys.

## 3. Starting a related-work section

**You want:** the foundational work for a topic, including papers from years
before your daily window.

```bash
uv run papertracker --project my-topic --related-work --facets --limit 40
```

`--related-work` ignores `--days` entirely and pulls citation-sorted candidates
across all years. `--facets` then splits the topic into 4–7 sub-themes and
selects round-robin across them, so one dominant sub-topic cannot swallow the
whole list.

You get two files: a `.facets.md` matrix grouped by facet, and a `.facets.json`
for programmatic use. Each candidate is annotated with a citation role —
`foundational`, `method`, `benchmark`, `contrast` — and a note on how it differs
from your stated contribution.

To spend nothing at all, configure `related_work_facets` in your profile and add
`--no-summarize`; PaperTracker then uses your facets with deterministic
annotations. See [Related-work mode](related-work.md).

## 4. Watching specific venues

**You want:** never to miss a CHI or TVCG paper, and to care less about the rest.

Define the venues once at the top level of `user_data/projects.toml` and every
profile inherits them:

```toml
[[priority_venues]]
name = "ACM CHI"
publisher = "acm"
patterns = ["CHI Conference on Human Factors", "CHI '"]

[[priority_venues]]
name = "IEEE TVCG"
publisher = "ieee"
patterns = ["Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics"]
rss = "https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/rss/TOC2945.XML"
```

Those venues now (a) badge matching papers with `★` and sort them to the top of
the digest, (b) enable `--priority-venues-only`, and (c) add an RSS source that
often lands a day or two before the Crossref deposit.

```bash
uv run papertracker --priority-venues-only --days 7
```

## 5. Running without spending any quota

**You want:** the discovery and filtering, none of the AI cost.

`--no-summarize` is a complete workflow, not a diagnostic mode. Discovery,
dedup, and local relevance scoring all still run; only the summarization step is
skipped. Nothing is sent to an AI provider.

```bash
uv run papertracker --no-summarize --days 7                  # today's matches
uv run papertracker --no-summarize --threshold -1 --days 14  # every score, for calibration
```

The second form keeps everything regardless of score, which is the fastest way
to see where your threshold should sit.

This also composes with related-work mode when facets are preconfigured — see
[case 3](#3-starting-a-related-work-section).
